title: Safe Drywall Handling and Lifting
osha_standards: OSH Act Section 5(a)(1) General Duty Clause
summary: Drywall sheets are heavy and bulky, so bending, twisting, and lifting them causes serious overexertion injuries. This talk covers staging, team lifts, lifting tools, and the 50-pound limit.
talking_points: Stage drywall as close as possible to where it will be installed.
Lift with your leg muscles and do not twist while carrying. Plan the lift, clear the path, and face the direction you are walking.
Lift only one sheet at a time. Never lift more than 50 pounds by yourself - use two workers for larger, thicker, heavier sheets.
Use lifting tools, carts, or a panel hoist instead of carrying sheets by hand.
Use a vertical lift to hold drywall against the ceiling so you can screw it off more safely.
For vertical hanging: raise the sheet, shift your grip to opposite sides, rotate it upright, then secure it to the wall. Keep material and tools stored neatly to prevent trips.
site_hazards_to_check: Drywall stacked far from the install area, forcing long carries
Stairs, ramps, or cluttered paths on the carry route
Single workers carrying large or ceiling sheets alone
No carts, panel hoist, or lifting tools available
Material and offcuts piled in walkways
discussion_questions: How close can we stage the board to where it is going?
Which sheets today need two people or a lift?
What lifting tools are on site, and who knows how to use them?

flags: Non-blocking: the 50-lb single-person figure is NIOSH lifting guidance, not an OSHA regulatory limit. Wording ('Never lift more than 50 pounds by yourself') is acceptable as a rule of thumb. OSHA authority is correctly the General Duty Clause (no specific manual-handling standard) plus 1926.250 for material storage/staging.
